solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Drinks apostle chucked over bishop

definitions.note: plural noun, matching the plural answer

indicators.note: something chucked over is tossed about, so the letters of apostle and the bishop's letter land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A furious disciple of Christ hurls something over a bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop.
explanation.definitionFit: Potables are things fit for drinking, a slightly formal noun for beverages.

clue.text: Forbearance needed in hearing for cases

indicators.note: in hearing means the word is spoken and the spelling chosen is a different word that sounds the same

parts.note: patience is forbearance, tolerance of delay

explanation.surface: A judge needs patience during a court hearing of legal cases.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' and 'cases' set up a courtroom, but the cases are a doctor's, not a judge's.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor speaks of the people under treatment as cases, so patients fits.

clue.text: Stud who once freshly-cultivated lands

indicators.note: ground freshly cultivated is turned over, so these letters are dug up into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A stud farm that once had freshly ploughed fields.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lands' looks like a noun for fields; it is the verb, as an aircraft does.
explanation.definitionFit: An aeroplane that touches down comes back to the runway, the idiom for landing.

clue.text: New pub's motto?

indicators.note: new signals the letters made new, rearranged into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A pub just opened wants a catchy motto.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the anagram and the definition: the toast urging everyone to drain their glass would suit a pub as its slogan.
explanation.definitionFit: The drinking toast urges people to empty their glasses, a fitting slogan for any pub.

clue.text: Resin priest inhales close to comatose male

indicators.note: what is inhaled is drawn inside, so the priest's name takes the other letters into its middle

parts.note: Eli is the priest of Shiloh who raised Samuel in the Bible

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the close of comatose is its last letter

explanation.surface: A priest breathes in fumes near a comatose man.
explanation.walkthrough: Eli is the crossword's favourite priest, from the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Elemi is a fragrant gum from tropical trees, used in varnishes and incense.

clue.text: Start to knit dark jumper

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the start of knit is its first letter
night is the dark, as in after dark

explanation.surface: Someone begins knitting a dark sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' is British for a sweater, which suits knitting; here it is the chess piece that leaps over others.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess the knight is the only piece that leaps over others, hence a jumper.

clue.text: On no account head to Norwich at any time

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the head of Norwich is its first letter
ever means at any time, as in 'if ever'

explanation.surface: Someone vows never to go to Norwich, whatever the time.
explanation.definitionFit: Never and on no account both express an absolute refusal, interchangeable as adverbs.

clue.text: Gran's regularly denied flatulence

indicators.note: letters denied at a regular interval leave every other one, starting with the first

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Grandma routinely denies that she has wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Gas is the everyday word for wind in the gut, the medical sense of flatulence.

clue.text: Amount to nothing in race with a liberal

indicators.note: nothing goes in the race, its letter sitting inside

parts.note: the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man
O looks like zero
taken as written

explanation.surface: A liberal's efforts in a race come to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amount to nothing' reads as one phrase; the definition is only 'Amount', with 'to' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A total is the full sum or amount reached by adding things up.

clue.text: Munitions men with knight found amongst set of steps

parts.note: OR is other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

indicators.note: a thing found amongst others sits within them, so the knight's letter goes inside the steps

parts.note: a dance is a set sequence of steps

explanation.surface: Weapons and soldiers, with a knight, turn up on a staircase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set of steps' suggests stairs; it is a dance. N is the chess notation for knight.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordnance is military supplies, especially artillery and ammunition, collectively munitions.

clue.text: Street drug taken by loyal board member

indicators.note: the street and drug are taken in by the word for loyal, which holds them inside

parts.note: true means faithful, loyal
E is ecstasy

explanation.surface: A street drug is taken by a faithful company director.
explanation.definitionFit: Trustees sit on a board that governs a charity or trust.

clue.text: Vicar one's relations call on again

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend, is a vicar's title
one is I, and one's is 'one is', I'S
it is slang for sex, and relations here means sexual relations

explanation.surface: A vicar's relatives drop in on him again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relations' looks like family; it is the sexual sense, which crosswords give as IT.
explanation.definitionFit: To revisit is to visit or call on someone a second time.

clue.text: African in Haiti open to change

indicators.note: the letters are open to change, so they may be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An African living in Haiti is open to change.
explanation.definitionFit: An Ethiopian is a person from Ethiopia in the Horn of Africa.

clue.text: Short and long rivers in the countryside

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase, matching the adjective rural

parts.note: a short river is just its abbreviation, R
the Ural is a long river, one of the rivers the clue names

explanation.surface: Rivers short and long run through the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rivers' serves both: a short one is R, a long one the Ural, running from Russia to the Caspian.
explanation.definitionFit: Rural describes places out in the country rather than the town.

clue.text: Needing resolution, enter talks with a venomous type

indicators.note: letters needing resolution have to be sorted out into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poisonous character is drawn into negotiations that need settling.
explanation.definitionFit: A rattlesnake is a venomous American pit viper with a rattling tail.

clue.text: Inquire in empty supermarket about jobs

indicators.note: the question word sits in the emptied, turned shop
about here means turned round, so the two outer letters are read in the opposite order
an empty word loses its contents, leaving its first and last letters

parts.note: an empty supermarket keeps only its outer letters
to ask is to inquire

explanation.surface: A shopper asks about jobs in a deserted supermarket.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasks are pieces of work to be done, jobs.

clue.text: Tory laws broken by tense associates

indicators.note: the words are broken open and the tense's letter pushed into the gap

parts.note: CON is short for Conservative
acts of Parliament are laws

explanation.surface: Conservative laws are broken by people under strain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like an adjective for nervous; it is the grammar term, abbreviated T.
explanation.definitionFit: Contacts are people you know and can call on, business associates.

clue.text: Clubs worrying about Hearts playing away from home

definitions.note: a verb phrase, matching the participle

indicators.note: the clubs and worrying letters go about the hearts, enclosing it

parts.note: eating means worrying, as in 'what's eating you?'

explanation.surface: Football clubs fret over Hearts, who are playing an away fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts is a Scottish football club, so the surface reads as sport; 'playing away from home' is the idiom for being unfaithful. C and H are the card suits.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone playing away is having an affair, so cheating on their partner.

clue.text: Praiseworthy officer saves British ensign at front

indicators.note: to save is to keep safe inside, so the officer holds the British letter

parts.note: an admiral is a senior naval officer

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the front of ensign is its first letter

explanation.surface: A naval officer rescues a British flag at the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ensign' suggests a naval flag or junior officer, matching the admiral; only its first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Admirable means deserving admiration, worthy of praise.

clue.text: Gatecrasher's more uncivil chasing popular model

parts.note: in means fashionable, popular
the Model T was Ford's famous car
ruder means more impolite

explanation.surface: The gatecrasher is ruder than the fashionable model he follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chasing' means coming after, so the ruder part follows the other two; the 's is 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A gatecrasher turns up uninvited, an intruder on the party.

clue.text: Old container of meat and two veg?

definitions.text: Old container of meat and two veg?

parts.note: a historical item that held something, here a pouch worn at the front of breeches
British slang for the male genitals, borrowing the name of a plain dinner

explanation.walkthrough: Meat and two veg is a traditional British plate of food, and also a jokey term for a man's private parts, which the Tudor garment covered.
explanation.definitionFit: A codpiece was a flap or pouch covering the groin in men's breeches of the 15th and 16th centuries.

clue.text: Chap snarfing one slice of lamb in Italian place

indicators.note: to snarf is to wolf food down, so the chap swallows the other letters inside him

parts.note: a man is a chap
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: a single slice is just the first letter

parts.note: one slice of lamb is its first letter

explanation.surface: A man gobbles a slice of lamb in an Italian city.
explanation.definitionFit: Milan is the major city of Lombardy in northern Italy.

clue.text: Bloody busy bloke I see on blower

parts.note: a bloke is a man
taken as written

indicators.note: blower is British slang for the telephone, so the word is heard, not seen, and its sound-alike letter is used

parts.note: the word see is spoken, sounding like the letter C

explanation.surface: A frantic man says 'I see' down the telephone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blower' is old British slang for the phone, so 'see' is spoken and becomes the letter C. 'Bloody' is a British intensifier.
explanation.definitionFit: Manic means frenziedly busy, full of wild energy.

clue.text: Day in which a soprano makes complaints

indicators.note: the day is the thing in which the letter a is placed

parts.note: MON is short for Monday
taken as written

explanation.surface: A day on which a singer airs her grievances.
explanation.definitionFit: Moans are grumbles, complaints made in a whining way.

clue.text: Relax in church? Slormgorm will!

parts.note: the setter is speaking, so Slormgorm will is 'I will', shortened to I'LL

explanation.surface: The setter promises to unwind during a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by name; here the name stands for I, so 'Slormgorm will' is I'll.
explanation.definitionFit: To chill, or chill out, is slang for to relax.

clue.text: I suppose he runs riot with rioters

definitions.note: a speaker's phrase standing for one who supposes

indicators.note: letters that run riot are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone guesses that a man is running wild alongside a mob.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: the person who says 'I suppose' is one who forms theories.
explanation.definitionFit: A theoriser speculates and proposes ideas, someone forever supposing.

clue.text: Contrary Tyneside fellow with back towards you

indicators.note: contrary means the other way round, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: Tyneside is in the North East of England, NE
a don is a university fellow

explanation.surface: A contrary Geordie turns his back on you.
explanation.walkthrough: A Geordie is a person from Tyneside, in north-east England, which sets up the surface; only NE is used.
explanation.definitionFit: End on describes something positioned with its end, here its back end, facing the viewer.

clue.text: Union must stop legal proceeding in Sale

indicators.note: to stop is to plug a gap, so the union's letter goes inside the lawsuit

parts.note: an action is a lawsuit

explanation.surface: A trade union must halt a court case in the town of Sale.
explanation.walkthrough: Sale is a town near Manchester, which disguises the definition with a capital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An auction is a public sale where goods go to the highest bidder.

clue.text: Leaders in City Hall all drink

indicators.note: the leaders are the first letters of each word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The heads of City Hall all have a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Cha is British slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Cha, or char, is colloquial British for tea, the national drink.

clue.text: Lawyer at bar snorting heroin and whizz

parts.note: DA is a District Attorney

indicators.note: snorting draws a drug inside, so the stripe takes the heroin letter in

parts.note: a band is a stripe or bar

explanation.surface: A barrister snorts heroin and speed in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whizz' is slang for amphetamine, which fits the drug scene; here it means an expert.
explanation.definitionFit: A dab hand is someone highly skilled at something, an expert.

clue.text: Bit of brouhaha in old Hackney house?

indicators.note: the bit of brouhaha is placed inside the word for old

parts.note: stale means old, no longer fresh

indicators.note: a bit is just the first letter

parts.note: a bit of brouhaha is its first letter

explanation.surface: A spot of commotion in an old house in Hackney, east London.
explanation.walkthrough: Hackney looks like the London borough; a hackney is a horse kept for riding or driving.
explanation.definitionFit: A stable is the building where horses are housed.

clue.text: Fly won't open next to private part of body

parts.note: inner means private, as in inner thoughts

indicators.note: the word won't open, losing its first letter

parts.note: to fly is to tear, rush off

explanation.surface: A trouser fly refuses to open beside someone's private parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' suggests trousers and 'private' private parts; both are innocent verbs and adjectives here.
explanation.definitionFit: The inner ear is the deep part of the ear containing the cochlea and balance organs.
